彈撥爾以其溫潤而富有穿透力的音色著稱。其音質介於明亮與暗沉之間，帶有獨特的金屬質: The tanbur is known for a warm timbre that carries well. Its tone falls between bright and dark, with a distinctive metallic edge and warm resonance. It is most at home from the middle to the upper register and can produce clear, expressive notes. When a string is plucked the body resonates deeply; the tone is crispest at the start and then fades into a warm tail. Compared with the bright, clean sound of the Western classical guitar, the tanbur sounds more Eastern and more weighty; compared with the pipa it is softer and more delicate, lacking the pipa's sharp attack. Its way of resonating is distinctive, producing continuous layers of resonance between plucks, which gives the music flow and poetic expressiveness.
彈撥爾多為木製長頸魯特琴。庫爾德彈撥爾共鳴箱常以七至十片肋板黏合，面板桑木，琴頸: The tanbur is mostly a wooden long-necked lute. The Kurdish tanbur's soundbox is often built from seven to ten glued ribs, with a mulberry soundboard and a walnut neck, strung with metal; the Afghan tanbur has a body carved from a single piece of mulberry, with metal strings and a metal-wire plectrum; the Tajik/Uzbek tanbur has a body hollowed out of mulberry, with a neck that may be inlaid with bone or white plastic. The Turkish tambur has a round body of about twenty to twenty-five thin wooden ribs and metal strings; its bowed form may have a soundbox of metal or wood, faced with skin or acrylic film. The Pamiri tanbur is carved from mulberry or apricot, with a goatskin or sheepskin soundboard and nylon strings. The source does not state the materials of the remaining parts.
彈撥爾為弦鳴樂器，屬長頸魯特琴類。它見於伊朗、伊拉克、印度、亞美尼亞、阿富汗、亞: The tanbur is a chordophone of the long-necked lute class. It appears in the traditional music of Iran, Iraq, India, Armenia, Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Pakistan, Turkey, Tajikistan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan; the Kurdish tanbur is used in Ahl-e Haqq (Yarsani) ritual and in the Kurdish Sufi music of western Iran, the Afghan tanbur can accompany song and dance or, less often, perform the classical ghazal, and in the Qing court's Hui repertoire it was also called danbuer.
彈撥爾為長頸弦鳴樂器，名稱可指多種相關魯特琴。其形制可追溯至美索不達米亞阿卡德時: The tanbur is a long-necked chordophone, and the name can refer to several related lutes. Its form can be traced to the Akkadian period in Mesopotamia, in the third millennium BC; a clay figure from Susa of 1500 BC and a rock carving at Mosul of about 1000 BC both show similar instruments. Its name appears in Parthian and Sassanian documents. In the tenth century al-Farabi distinguished a Baghdadi and a Khorasani type, the latter perhaps the ancestor of the instruments of northern Iraq, Syria, Iran, Sindh and Turkey. The name passed through Arabia into Europe, giving the tambura, the domra and the bandura, while in India it denotes the tanpura. It came to China in the Han dynasty and later developed into the Tang pipa; in the Qing dynasty it was called danbuer and included in the Hui repertoire.
彈撥爾（Tanbur）是一組長頸撥弦樂器，屬弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sa: The tanbur is a group of long-necked plucked instruments, chordophones, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321. They share a slender neck and a soundbox, are mostly fretted lutes, commonly strung with metal, and played with the fingers or a plectrum. The name covers related instruments in the traditional music of Iran, Iraq, Turkey, the Caucasus, Central Asia and South Asia, used in folk and art music and also in religious ritual.
